SMTO-SKL-0075 — Microsoft 365 turned down SMTO's request

GUID: 4bcf08dd-7fef-5e6f-945d-d7a2b416faec
Slug: microsoft365-graph-error
Domain: SKL · Subsystem: microsoft365

What happened

  • Microsoft refused what SMTO asked it to do and gave an unusual reason SMTO doesn't recognize. SMTO can't be sure whether anything changed, so check before trying again.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Check whether your action already happened: open the email, event, contact or file in Outlook, OneDrive or SharePoint with the same Microsoft account. Microsoft's reason was unclear, so it's safest to look before asking SMTO to change anything again.
  2. If you were changing a file, make sure nobody has it open for editing and that your OneDrive or SharePoint isn't out of storage space. A locked file or a full storage space are common reasons Microsoft refuses a file change.
  3. If the change didn't happen, ask SMTO to try it once more. Some refusals are brief, and a single new attempt shows whether the problem remains.

What success looks like

  • SMTO completes the request and you can see the result in Outlook, OneDrive or SharePoint.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO's Microsoft 365 setup; the details include Microsoft's response number. Don't keep repeating a change you haven't confirmed.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Microsoft Graph returned an error HTTP status that SMTO does not classify specifically (not 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 412, 429 or 500/502/503/504) and supplied no recognized provider error code; the status is recorded in status_code.

What this means

  • Graph returns an error HTTP status outside its explicit classifications and supplies no recognized overriding provider code. This explanation performs no Microsoft request. The original operation stage and receipt determine its effect; keep the selected tenant, account and resource identity fixed during recovery.

Why this can happen

  • Graph returns an error HTTP status outside its explicit classifications and supplies no recognized overriding provider code.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the recorded status and safe provider evidence rather than guessing a permission or input cause.

How to fix it

  • Read status_code from the error result to identify the Graph condition, for example 423 locked item, 413 too large, 507 insufficient storage or 405 unsupported operation. Address that condition, inspect the target resource under the same account_ref before repeating any write, and report a reproducible unclassified status as an SMTO bug.
  • Use the recorded status to identify the provider condition; inspect prior effects before repeating any mutation.

Retry and execution caution

  • Inspect provider state and exact account authority first.

How to verify the fix

  • Recovery addresses the actual recorded provider condition before any new operation.

What not to do

  • Do not expose secrets or blindly replay uncertain mutations.

Technical notes

  • This explanation performs no Microsoft request. The original operation stage and receipt determine its effect; keep the selected tenant, account and resource identity fixed during recovery.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
